stem:
Ethanol is mixed with sodium amide. Which side of the equilibrium is favoured?
[[eq:CCO + [NH2-]>>CC[O-] + N]]

choices.why: Ethanol ({{pKa}} 16) is a far stronger acid than ammonia (38). The proton ends up on the stronger base, amide, and the equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid.
This has the rule backwards. The equilibrium does not keep the stronger acid and the stronger base: those are the two that react.
K is 1 only when the acids on the two sides have the same {{pKa}}, as in water with hydroxide. Here they differ by 22 units.

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: On the left, the species that gives up a proton is ethanol. On the right, the species that would give it back is ammonia.

ask.a: Amide on the left, ethoxide on the right.

steps.h: Ethanol 16. Ammonia 38.
The stronger acid gives its proton to the stronger base. The equilibrium lies on the side with the weaker acid, the one with the higher {{pKa}}: the right.
K = 10<sup>(38 - 16)</sup> = 10<sup>22</sup>. The reaction goes to completion. The lecture's version with water in place of ethanol gives the same picture.

ask.q: Which is the weaker base, amide or ethoxide?
ask.a: Ethoxide. The favoured side always holds the weaker acid and the weaker base together.

solution.answer: The right side, with K about 10<sup>22</sup>
solution.rule: Equilibrium favours the side with the weaker acid (higher {{pKa}}).

stem:
Estimate the equilibrium constant. Write it as K = 10<sup>x</sup> and give x.
[[eq:C#C + [NH2-]>>[C-]#C + N]]

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: acetylene gives up the proton. Right: ammonia is the acid that would give it back.

ask.q: Which two numbers do you need?
ask.a: The {{pKa}} of acetylene and the {{pKa}} of ammonia.

steps.h: Acetylene 25. Ammonia 38.
x = {{pKa}} of the acid on the product side minus {{pKa}} of the acid on the reactant side = 38 - 25 = 13.

ask.q: How do you check the sign without the formula?
ask.a: The weaker acid, ammonia, is on the right, so the right is favoured and x must be positive.

steps.t: See where the formula comes from
steps.h: For each acid, {{Ka}} = 10<sup>-{{pKa}}</sup>. K for the proton transfer is {{Ka}} of the acid on the left divided by {{Ka}} of the acid on the right: 10<sup>-25</sup> / 10<sup>-38</sup> = 10<sup>13</sup>.

ask.q: What would x be for water with hydroxide?
ask.a: 0, so K = 1: the lecture's first example.

steps.h: K = 10<sup>13</sup>: amide removes the alkyne hydrogen completely. This is how acetylide ions are made.

solution.rule: K = 10<sup>({{pKa}} of product acid - {{pKa}} of reactant acid)</sup>.

stem:
Which base is strong enough to convert 1-butyne completely into its conjugate base?
[[mol:CCC#C]]

choices.why: The conjugate acid of amide is ammonia, {{pKa}} 38, far above 25. K = 10<sup>13</sup>: complete.
The conjugate acid of hydroxide is water, 15.7, which is a stronger acid than the alkyne (25). K = 10<sup>-9</sup>: almost nothing happens. The mistake is assuming any strong base will do.
tert-Butoxide is the strongest of the alkoxides, but its conjugate acid is only 17. Still eight units short of 25.
Acetate is a weak base: its conjugate acid, acetic acid, is 4.

steps.t: Find the acid and its value
steps.h: The acidic hydrogen of 1-butyne is the one on the {{sp}} carbon: 25.

ask.q: What must be true of a base that removes it completely?
ask.a: Its conjugate acid must be a weaker acid than the alkyne: {{pKa}} well above 25.

steps.t: Write the conjugate acid of each base
steps.h: Amide gives ammonia, 38. Hydroxide gives water, 15.7. tert-Butoxide gives tert-butanol, 17. Acetate gives acetic acid, 4.

ask.q: Which of these numbers is above 25?

steps.h: Only amide passes. For the others the equilibrium lies on the left, because the alkyne is the weaker acid.
A carbanion base would work as well: the conjugate acid of {{CH3Li}} is methane, 50 to 60.

ask.q: Would the acetylide ion survive in water?
ask.a: No. Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so water would put the proton straight back.

solution.rule: A base deprotonates an acid completely only if the base's conjugate acid has the higher {{pKa}}.

stem:
A drop of water falls into a flask of methylmagnesium bromide in diethyl ether. What happens, and why?
[[mol:C[Mg]Br]]

choices.h: The Grignard reagent takes a proton from water and becomes methane: the reagent is destroyed
choices.why: Think of the reagent as {{CH3-}} with {{MgBr+}}. The carbanion is a very strong base, and water (15.7) is an enormously stronger acid than methane (50 to 60). K is at least 10<sup>34</sup>.

choices.h: Nothing: water is too weak an acid to react
choices.why: Whether an acid is strong enough depends on the base it meets. Against a carbanion, water is a strong acid.

choices.h: Water acts as a nucleophile and replaces the bromine on magnesium, leaving the C-Mg bond intact
choices.why: This looks at the wrong part of the reagent. The reactive site is the carbon, which carries the electron density, and proton transfers are very fast.

choices.h: The Grignard reagent is in equilibrium with a little methane, K about 1
choices.why: K is 1 only when the two acids have the same {{pKa}}. Here they differ by 34 units or more.

steps.t: See the reagent as a base
steps.h: The C-Mg bond is polarized with the electron density on carbon. The lecture: think R:<sup>-</sup> with {{MgX+}}, a strong base.

ask.q: What is the conjugate acid of {{CH3-}}?

steps.h:
[[eqr:C[Mg]Br + O>>C + O[Mg]Br]]
The acid on the left is water. The acid on the right is methane.
Water 15.7, methane 50 to 60. The weaker acid is methane, so the right side is favoured.

ask.q: What is K if you use 50 for methane?

steps.h: The reaction is complete and cannot be undone: methane is a gas and leaves. Every molecule of water destroys one molecule of reagent.
Grignard reagents are made in dry diethyl ether and organolithium reagents in pentane: solvents with no O-H. Water or acid is added only in a separate step, after the reagent has done its job.

ask.q: Could ethanol be used as the solvent instead?
ask.a: No. Its O-H (16) is as destructive as water's.

solution.answer: The carbanion carbon takes H from water: {{CH4}} forms and the reagent is destroyed (K about 10<sup>34</sup> or more).
solution.rule: RMgX and RLi act as R:<sup>-</sup>, very strong bases: any O-H destroys them.

choices.why: Acetic acid (4) is a stronger acid than water (15.7). The weaker acid, water, is on the right. K is about 10<sup>12</sup>.

choices.h: The left: acetic acid and hydroxide
choices.why: The left holds the stronger acid and the stronger base. They react. The mistake is thinking the strong ones are the ones that remain.
The two acids differ by about twelve {{pKa}} units.

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: acetic acid. Right: water.
Acetic acid 4. Water 15.7.
The equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, water: the right. Hydroxide deprotonates a carboxylic acid completely.

solution.rule: The side with the higher {{pKa}} acid wins.

stem:
What is the equilibrium constant for this proton transfer?
[[eq:O + [OH-]>>[OH-] + O]]

choices.why: The acid on each side is water, {{pKa}} 15.7. The difference is zero and 10<sup>0</sup> = 1. This is the lecture's first example.
This uses one {{pKa}} alone. K for a proton transfer comes from the difference between the two acids.
That is {{Ka}} of water, the constant for water giving a proton to nothing in particular. Here the proton goes to hydroxide.

choices.h: K cannot be defined because nothing changes
choices.why: Protons really do hop between water and hydroxide. The two sides are simply equal in energy.

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Water on the left, water on the right.
K = 10<sup>0</sup> = 1: neither side is favoured.

solution.rule: Same acid on both sides: K = 1.

stem:
Estimate K = 10<sup>x</sup> for this reaction and give x. Use 4 for the carboxylic acid and 16 for the alcohol.
[[eq:CC(=O)O + CC[O-]>>CC(=O)[O-] + CCO]]

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: acetic acid, 4. Right: ethanol, 16.

steps.t: Subtract product acid minus reactant acid

steps.h: The weaker acid, ethanol, is on the right, so the right is favoured and x is positive: K = 10<sup>12</sup>.

solution.rule: x = {{pKa}} (acid on the right) minus {{pKa}} (acid on the left).

stem: For each equilibrium, say which side is favoured.

items.why: H-Cl (-8) is a stronger acid than {{H3O+}} (-1.5). The weaker acid is on the right.
Acetic acid (4) is a weaker acid than {{H3O+}} (-1.5). The weaker acid is on the left: acetic acid is mostly not ionized in water.
Ammonia as an acid is 38. Water is 15.7. The weaker acid, ammonia, is on the left: hydroxide cannot make amide.
Acetylene (25) is a stronger acid than ammonia (38). The weaker acid is on the right.
Methanol 15.5 and ethanol 15.9 are the same within half a unit: a mixture of both alkoxides, K close to 1.

steps.t: Find the two acids in each line
steps.h: One on each side: the species that holds the proton being passed.
H-Cl -8, {{H3O+}} -1.5, acetic acid 4, water 15.7, alcohols about 16, acetylene 25, ammonia 38.
The side that holds the acid with the higher {{pKa}} is the favoured side. When the two values are nearly equal, neither side wins.

solution.rule: Find the two acids, compare their {{pKa}} values, favour the weaker acid.

stem:
Sodium hydroxide is added to 1-butyne. Estimate K = 10<sup>x</sup> and give x to the nearest whole number. Mind the sign.
[[eq:CCC#C + [OH-]>>CCC#[C-] + O]]

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: the alkyne C-H, 25. Right: water, 15.7.

steps.t: Subtract product acid minus reactant acid

steps.h: The exponent is negative: K = 10<sup>-9</sup>. The weaker acid, the alkyne, is on the left, so almost nothing is deprotonated.
Hydroxide is not strong enough for a terminal alkyne. Sodium amide is (38 - 25 = +13).

solution.rule: A negative exponent means the reactants are favoured: the base is too weak.

stem: Which of these bases is not strong enough to convert phenol ({{pKa}} 10) into phenoxide? [[mol:Oc1ccccc1]]

choices.why: The conjugate acid of acetate is acetic acid, {{pKa}} 4, a stronger acid than phenol. The equilibrium lies on the phenol side, K = 10<sup>-6</sup>.

Hydroxide is strong enough. Its conjugate acid, water, is 15.7, above 10: K is about 10<sup>6</sup>. The mistake is treating phenol like an ordinary alcohol (16), which hydroxide only partly deprotonates.
Methoxide is strong enough: methanol is 15.5, above 10.
Amide is far more than strong enough: ammonia is 38.

steps.h: A base works if its conjugate acid has a higher {{pKa}} than the acid to be deprotonated, here 10.
Acetic acid 4, water 15.7, methanol 15.5, ammonia 38.
Only acetic acid is below 10. Acetate is the weaker base and phenol keeps its proton.

solution.rule: Compare the {{pKa}} of the acid with the {{pKa}} of the base's conjugate acid.

stem:
Ethanethiol has a {{pKa}} of about 10.5. Sort each base by whether it would convert the thiol essentially completely into its conjugate base.
[[mol:CCS]]

items.why: Conjugate acid water, 15.7: five units above 10.5, K about 10<sup>5</sup>.
Conjugate acid ammonia, 38: far more than enough.
Conjugate acid acetic acid, 4: a stronger acid than the thiol, so the proton stays on sulfur.
Conjugate acid H-F, 4. Fluoride is the strongest base of the halides but still a weak base.
Conjugate acid H-Br, -9: bromide is hardly a base at all.

steps.h: The base's conjugate acid must have a {{pKa}} above 10.5, and a few units above for the reaction to be complete.
Water 15.7, methanol 15.5, ammonia 38, acetic acid 4, H-F 4, H-Br -9.
Above 10.5: hydroxide, methoxide, amide. Below: acetate, fluoride, bromide.

steps.t: Notice the contrast with an alcohol
steps.h: Hydroxide deprotonates a thiol completely but an alcohol (16) only partly, because the thiol is five to six units more acidic.

solution.rule: For every base, ask for the {{pKa}} of its conjugate acid.

stem: Which liquid can be used as the solvent for making a Grignard reagent from bromoethane and magnesium?

choices.why: Diethyl ether has no acidic hydrogen: only C-H bonds, and oxygen with lone pairs. It is the lecture's solvent for R-X + Mg.
Ethanol has an O-H, {{pKa}} 16. The Grignard carbon would take that proton and become ethane. The mistake is thinking only water is a problem.
Water, {{pKa}} 15.7, protonates the reagent as fast as it forms: R:<sup>-</sup> + H-OH gives R-H.
Acetic acid, {{pKa}} 4, is an even stronger acid than water and destroys the reagent at once.

steps.t: Treat the reagent as a base
steps.h: {{CH3CH2MgBr}} behaves as {{CH3CH2-}}: the conjugate base of ethane, {{pKa}} 50 to 60.

steps.t: Check each solvent for an acidic hydrogen
steps.h: Ethanol 16, water 15.7, acetic acid 4: each is an enormously stronger acid than ethane, so each would protonate the carbanion. Diethyl ether has no O-H.
Diethyl ether. The same reasoning makes pentane the solvent for organolithium reagents.

solution.rule: No O-H, N-H or S-H anywhere near RMgX or RLi.

stem:
Methyllithium is added to 1-butyne. What happens?
[[mol:[Li]C]] [[mol:CCC#C]]

choices.why: {{CH3Li}} acts as {{CH3-}}, a very strong base. The alkyne C-H (25) is a far stronger acid than methane (50 to 60), so the proton is transferred: K is 10<sup>25</sup> or more. Methane bubbles off.

choices.h: No reaction: a hydrocarbon has no acidic hydrogen
choices.why: A terminal alkyne has one, {{pKa}} 25. Whether it counts as acidic depends on the base, and a carbanion is the strongest base there is.
This has the methyl group adding across the triple bond. A fast proton transfer is available, and acid-base reactions come first.
This removes a {{CH2}} hydrogen. The hydrogen on the {{sp}} carbon (25) is the acidic one, as in propyne on the exam.

steps.h: The C-Li bond is polarized toward carbon: think {{CH3-}} and {{Li+}}.
1-Butyne has a hydrogen on an {{sp}} carbon, {{pKa}} 25.

steps.t: Compare with the conjugate acid of the base
steps.h: Methane is 50 to 60. The alkyne is the stronger acid by at least 25 units, so the equilibrium lies completely on the side of methane and the lithium acetylide.
A terminal alkyne is one more group that an organolithium or Grignard reagent cannot coexist with. It is also a clean way to make an acetylide.

solution.answer: Proton transfer: methane and the lithium acetylide
solution.rule: Organometallics are bases first: look for any hydrogen with a {{pKa}} below about 50.

stem:
Estimate K = 10<sup>x</sup> for the reaction of methyllithium with water and give x to the nearest whole number. Use 50 for methane.
[[eq:[Li]C + O>>C + [Li+].[OH-]]]
note: The lecture gives 50 to 60 for an alkane, so any exponent from 34 to 44 is consistent with it. The question fixes methane at 50.

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: water gives up the proton, 15.7. Right: methane is the conjugate acid of the base {{CH3-}}, 50 with the value given.

steps.t: Subtract product acid minus reactant acid

steps.h: K is about 10<sup>34</sup>. With the lecture's upper value of 60 for an alkane it would be 10<sup>44</sup>. Either way the reaction is complete.
This is the lecture's reason for calling organolithium reagents very strong bases, and the reason water must be kept away from them.

solution.rule: Water against a carbanion: K of at least 10<sup>34</sup>.

stem:
Isopropylmagnesium bromide is treated with {{D2O}} (D is deuterium, a heavy hydrogen that reacts as H does). What is the organic product?
[[rxn:CC(C)[Mg]Br>D2O>"?"]]

choices.why: The carbon bonded to magnesium is the carbanion. It takes a D from {{D2O}}, exactly as it would take an H from water, so D ends up where Mg was: on the middle carbon.
Plain propane is what {{H2O}} gives. The proton, here a deuteron, comes from the acid that is added, and that acid is {{D2O}}.
This treats {{D2O}} as a source of oxygen. With a Grignard reagent, water is an acid: the carbon takes D, not OD.
D on an end carbon. The new C-D bond forms at the carbon that carried the magnesium, the middle one. Nothing moves along the chain.

steps.t: Treat the reagent as a base
steps.h: {{(CH3)2CHMgBr}} acts as the carbanion {{(CH3)2CH-}}, with the lone pair on the middle carbon.
{{D2O}} is water with D in place of H. Its {{pKa}} is essentially that of water, enormously below the 50 to 60 of propane.
The carbanion takes D. The product is propane with one D on the middle carbon, 2-deuteriopropane.
This is the last step of the lecture's synthesis from propene: add H-Br, make the Grignard with Mg in ether, then {{D2O}} for the deuterated product or {{H2O}} for plain propane.

solution.rule: {{D2O}} puts a D exactly where the metal was.

choices.h: The right: the acids are {{CH3NH3+}} (about 10.5) and water (15.7)
choices.why: The ammonium ion is the acid on the left and water is the acid on the right. Water is the weaker acid, so the right is favoured, with K about 10<sup>5</sup>.

choices.h: The left: an amine is 38 and water is 15.7
choices.why: 38 is the {{pKa}} of the neutral amine losing an N-H to become {{CH3NH-}}. That is not this reaction. Here the acid is the charged ammonium ion. This is the exam's amine trap moved into an equilibrium.

choices.h: The left: hydroxide is a strong base and stays as it is
choices.why: A strong base is exactly the species that takes the proton. Strength means it reacts.
The two acids differ by about five units.

steps.t: Find the acid on each side
steps.h: Left: {{CH3NH3+}} gives up a proton and becomes the neutral amine. Right: water would give it back.

steps.t: Use the value for the species drawn
steps.h: The ammonium ion, with its positive charge, is about 10 to 11. Water is 15.7.
Water is the weaker acid, so the equilibrium lies to the right: hydroxide frees an amine from its ammonium salt.

solution.rule: Use the {{pKa}} of the acid exactly as drawn: {{RNH3+}} is about 10.5, {{RNH2}} is 38.

stem: Which statement about an acid-base equilibrium is correct?

choices.h: It favours the side with the weaker acid and the weaker base
choices.why: The stronger acid and the stronger base are the pair that react. What they make, the weaker acid and the weaker base, is what collects.

choices.h: It favours the side with the stronger acid
choices.why: The stronger acid is the one more willing to lose its proton, so it is used up.

choices.h: It favours the side with the acid of lower {{pKa}}
choices.why: Lower {{pKa}} means stronger acid. This is the same mistake as above, written with numbers.
The direction depends on the two {{pKa}} values. Hydroxide with ammonia, for example, stays on the left.

steps.h: Every proton transfer has an acid and a base on each side, and they are conjugate pairs: the weaker acid sits with the weaker base.
Weaker acid and weaker base means more stable species. An equilibrium collects on the more stable side.
Water (15.7) with amide gives hydroxide and ammonia (38). The lecture: lies to the right, the side with ammonia, the weaker acid.

solution.answer: The side with the weaker acid and weaker base

stem: For each equilibrium, say which side is favoured. Several are written to mislead.

items.why: {{H2S}} (10) is a stronger acid than methanol (15.5). The weaker acid is on the right. The trap is treating S-H like O-H.
Phenol (10) is a weaker acid than acetic acid (4). The weaker acid is on the left: acetate cannot deprotonate phenol.
tert-Butanol (17.0) is a weaker acid than methanol (15.5) in solution. K is about 10<sup>-1.5</sup>, so the left is favoured, though not by much.
H-F (4) is a much weaker acid than H-Cl (-8). Chloride is far too weak a base to take a proton from H-F.
Ammonia (38) is a weaker acid than acetylene (25). Acetylide is not a strong enough base to make amide. It is the reverse reaction that goes.
Acetylene (25) is a far stronger acid than methane (50 to 60). The weaker acid is on the right.

steps.t: Find the two acids in each line
steps.h: Do not judge by which species looks reactive. Find the proton that moves and the two species that hold it.
H-Cl -8, acetic acid 4, H-F 4, {{H2S}} 10, phenol 10, methanol 15.5, tert-butanol 17.0, acetylene 25, ammonia 38, methane 50 to 60.
In each line the side with the higher {{pKa}} is favoured.
tert-Butanol and methanol differ by only 1.5 units, so both alkoxides are present in real amounts. The others are one-sided.

solution.answer: Right, left, left, left, left, right
solution.rule: The side holding the acid with the higher {{pKa}} is favoured, however the equation is written.
